summary:
Lunar Landing Site Planner is a web app that answers one question: where and when can a lander touch down near the Moon's south pole and still have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio?
At the pole the Sun skims the horizon and ridges hide both the Sun and Earth, so the right site depends on the date. Our tool checks 23 sites, including NASA's nine Artemis candidate regions, hour by hour for 2027–2028. It uses NASA JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions, which our app matches to within 0.012°, against real terrain skylines from NASA's LOLA laser altimeter. A scorecard gives GO / NO-GO against NASA's 10° landing-slope limit using NASA's 20 m terrain, and shows how accurate that data is. Users can compare sites on a two-year calendar, inspect real slope-coloured 3D ground with live Sun shading, test mast heights and battery survival, and download the evidence as GIS, table and 3D files.
It turns NASA's open data into a transparent, checkable first screen for landing decisions, with its limits stated on screen.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Planner is a desktop web application that helps mission planners compare potential lunar landing sites and dates, especially near the Moon’s south pole.

What it does and how it works

Users select one or more lunar sites and a mission date. The planner then shows:

  • Sun and Earth positions against the local lunar terrain horizon
  • Sunlight and darkness periods for power generation
  • Earth-visibility periods for communications
  • Countdown to the next sunset and Earthset
  • Terrain slope, elevation, uncertainty, and permanently shadowed-region information
  • Site comparisons and GO/NO-GO indicators
  • Alternative dates and nearby sites when a selected mission window fails
  • Downloadable charts, terrain data, and site packages

The system uses precomputed scientific data stored as static JSON files, so it requires no backend or database. The Python pipeline generates the data, while the browser presents it interactively.

Benefits

The project converts complex lunar-environment data into a fast, visual decision-support tool. It helps users:

  • Compare sites in seconds rather than manually inspecting separate datasets
  • Identify reliable sunlight for solar power
  • Check communication availability with Earth
  • Understand terrain and landing-safety constraints
  • Quickly recover from a missed or unsuitable mission date
  • Explain technical results to non-specialists through the Learn/Explain interface

Intended impact

The intended impact is to support safer and more practical lunar mission planning. The tool can help researchers, educators, students, and mission teams understand how terrain, sunlight, communications, and landing requirements interact at different lunar locations.

It also encourages transparent decision-making by showing the evidence behind each recommendation rather than presenting an unexplained score.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

Frontend

  • Next.js 16 with the App Router
  • TypeScript with strict typing
  • React and Tailwind CSS
  • Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for 3D terrain views
  • Motion for animation
  • Zustand for interface state
  • Canvas and SVG for charts

Science and data pipeline

  • Python 3.12+
  • NASA/JPL Horizons and the DE441 ephemeris
  • Skyfield for independent validation
  • NumPy
  • Rasterio for lunar terrain data
  • NASA LRO/LOLA elevation and terrain products

Data sources

  • NASA/JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions
  • NASA LRO/LOLA for lunar elevation, slope, and terrain horizons
  • NASA and USGS sources for Artemis candidate regions
  • Published lunar-site coordinates and mission datasets

The application is designed for desktop browsers at 1280 pixels wide or larger and is hosted as a static web application.

What makes it creative

The project combines several normally separate planning views into one interactive workflow:

  • A sky and terrain visualization
  • Time-based sunlight and communications timelines
  • Mission-oriented scorecards
  • Multi-site comparison
  • Rescue recommendations for failed dates
  • Real terrain data rather than purely illustrative terrain
  • Exportable scientific evidence and terrain packages

A key creative element is the “rescue” experience: instead of simply reporting that a site/date fails, the application searches for nearby dates or alternative locations that satisfy the mission constraints.

Factors considered by the team

The team considered:

  • Scientific accuracy and independent validation
  • Real lunar terrain instead of invented or simplified values
  • Power and communications availability
  • Landing slope and EVA safety constraints
  • Terrain-data uncertainty
  • Differences between short-term date-specific visibility and long-term lunar averages
  • Clear separation between real data and illustrative visualization
  • Accessibility and plain-language explanations
  • Fast comparison for mission planning
  • Honest handling of missing data and sites outside terrain coverage
  • Reproducibility, downloadable evidence, and transparent data credits
  • Performance while displaying large time-series datasets

The project’s product definition and technical decisions are documented in the README.md, while the scientific sources are listed in pipeline/DATA.md.
